To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Arf6 and Cav1 regulate α6β4 recycling and HD growth in a mechano-dependent manner, thus linking HDs to the mechanoresponse of the cell.

(i) α6β4 recycling requires the Arf6 and GIT1/βPix GEF complex, but not caveolae; (ii) Arf6 and caveolin1 are required to remodel HDs in response to mechanical strain; (iii) Arf6 is required to maintain caveolin1 levels at the plasma membrane; (iv) Arf6, but not caveolin1, is required to maintain the levels of α6β4 at the cell edges.
Arf6, GIT1/βPix, and caveolae are involved in the mechanical remodeling of hemidesmosomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that link HDs to the mechanoresponse, and the role of caveolae and Arfs in this process.
the role of Arf6 and caveolae in HD remodeling.
how HDs respond and adapt to mechanical stress.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HD growth and remodeling involves Arf6-activated endocytosis of α6β4, and that this process is modulated by the mechano-sensing properties of caveolae.
the mechanical stress-induced HD growth is a process that involves the isotropic spreading of caveolae, which in turn is associated with integrin recycling and turnover.
Arf6 and caveolae regulate the mechanical stability of the HDs by regulating α6β4 turnover and localization at cell edges.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Arf6 and Cav1 are both required for HD growth, and that the latter is achieved through a mechano-response involving Arf6-dependent integrin recycling.
Arf6 and Cav1 regulate integrin trafficking in HDs and that this process is required for their remodeling in response to mechanical stress.
Arf6-activated integrin recycling is essential for HD remodeling and mechano-response.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HD remodeling pathway is a mechanosensitive process, which is distinct from the α6β4-dependent mechanoresponse.
the mechanoresponse of HDs involves a Cav1/Arf6-dependent pathway.
Arf6 and caveolae are essential for the mechanical remodeling of HDs.
